title: The Token Is Not the Right: Registry Authority and Economic Entitlement
subtitle: Separating economic claims, authoritative records, digital representations and settlement evidence
abstract: Tokenization is frequently presented as a single act of digitizing ownership. Financially, it consists of several legally and operationally distinct changes: an enforceable claim arises, a registry establishes the holder, a digital representation is issued, and a transfer or redemption changes the valid claim population. The proposed architecture makes those records explicit and independently reconcilable. It compares native on-ledger assets, custodian-backed receipts and derivative-like tokens without presuming that a wallet balance is legal title.

evidence.heading: What the published literature establishes
evidence.body: The BIS/CPMI 2024 tokenisation report approaches tokens as representations of money and other assets within programmable arrangements, while the IMF's 2025 framework evaluates market frictions over the full asset lifecycle. Neither definition makes a particular blockchain balance a universal substitute for legal ownership, custody, counterparty consent, or enforceable investor remedies. The FSB's 2024 assessment highlights legal and operational vulnerabilities that arise when the represented asset, venue, issuer and related intermediaries remain economically interconnected. Accordingly, a tokenization proposal should identify which record is authoritative at each transition and in each jurisdiction.

evidence.heading: Security ownership can differ from token control
evidence.body: The January 2026 SEC staff statement distinguishes tokenized securities arrangements by their issuer and intermediaries. An issuer-sponsored token may carry rights under a governing securities framework; a third-party representation may instead be an entitlement against another actor, and a synthetic exposure need not confer ownership in the referenced share. The staff statement is not binding law. The design implication for TSP-01 is architectural: do not infer from a cryptographic transfer that the legally required transfer agent, depository, custodian or beneficial-ownership register has changed.

evidence.heading: Registry authority and supply completeness
evidence.body: Token standards primarily specify contract interfaces and transfers; they do not determine the legal priority of the record of ownership. For a depositary receipt the custody account may be an independent source of backing, while for a loan claim the signed contract and servicing ledger may dominate. TSP-01's TRR should therefore keep separate immutable identifiers for obligation, economic owner, eligible quantity, token contract, settlement instruction, disputed quantity and redemption. Events must reconcile across these records without requiring every internal document or personally identifying fact to become public.

architecture.heading: Four-layer reference model
architecture.body: Layer 1 is the legally enforceable obligation or asset, identified by the issuing instrument and governing terms. Layer 2 is the authoritative rights register that determines permitted holders, units, encumbrances and restrictions. Layer 3 is the token representation, which can be held, transferred or constrained according to an interface standard. Layer 4 is the settlement and accounting evidence that establishes discharged obligations and treasury movements. Cross-layer links should be versioned and independently re-computable, including when an upstream asset record changes.

architecture.heading: A useful supply invariant
architecture.body: Define E as approved outstanding eligible economic interests, M as outstanding represented token units normalized to the economic denomination, and X as explicitly disclosed unrepresented interests. The design goal is E = M + X after accounting for partial settlements, redemption, disputed interests and the unit-conversion ratio. A stronger audit must also prove population completeness: all issuer obligations are included in E, not merely that the tokens already known to the auditor balance. A token smart contract cannot establish that its own issuer has declared every external liability.

architecture.heading: Native issuance, receipt, and derivative architectures
architecture.body: A native security may use the ledger as a legally authorized issuance and transfer record if the applicable law and governing rules permit it. A receipt architecture requires an issuer/custodian obligation backed by actual holdings and a redemption process. A derivative or synthetic token may create an exposure measured by an external price without conveying the underlying share. Compare the same user interface across these structures and the rights will differ substantially: voting, dividends, insolvency priority, collateral reuse and exchange privileges cannot be assumed equivalent.

architecture.heading: Event identity and accounting boundaries
architecture.body: Every registry mutation should reference the originating contract or corporate action, evidence of authorization, affected beneficial or legal holders, and the journal event if value has moved. Use separate event IDs for economic approvals, mint decisions, contract transfers, settlement finality and redemption, linked by a correlation ID. This avoids equating the token transaction hash with the entire commercial event and allows an auditor to reconstruct omissions and duplicates across systems.

case.title: Worked case: verified receivable tokenization
case.setup: Synthetic invoice of USD 100,000; USD 90,000 approved and USD 10,000 disputed. The approved amount is split 60% to a supplier and 40% to a financier. All amounts are illustrative and the claim is not a negotiable security merely by being tokenized.
rows: Supply linked to eligible rights, not original invoice
Token claim reduced to 60,000; signed finality receipts
Eligible claim becomes zero; 10,000 dispute remains separate
case.formula: Approved rights = 90,000; initial represented rights = 54,000 + 36,000. After first installment: 90,000 − 30,000 = 60,000 outstanding. Disputed 10,000 is never automatically minted.
case.interpretation: The exercise distinguishes an invoice, an approved payment obligation, the claim of each holder, the representation of that claim, and a completed monetary settlement. All five can change at different times.

risks: False issuance
Issuer mints 100,000 against only 90,000 verified eligibility; a naive on-chain supply check still passes against its own registry.
Independent claim verifier and reconciliation against the authoritative invoice approval population.
Divergent holders
A token transfer succeeds but the contract requires consent before assigning the receivable.
Legal assignment state gating and an exception ledger; do not advertise unconditional transfer rights.
Incomplete redemption
Cash is paid but the claim tokens remain transferable, inviting double claim presentation.
Atomic or coordinated cancellation with receipt and delayed-settlement lock states.
tests: Simulate approved, disputed, assigned and redeemed rights without allowing a negative or unsupported claim quantity.
Reconstruct legal and beneficial positions from registry updates, token transfers and journal entries with one deliberately missing event.
Compare native issuance, custody-backed receipt and synthetic token under insolvency and corporate-action scenarios.
conclusion: The most important property of a tokenization system is not token issuance speed; it is whether every represented unit corresponds to a well-defined, enforceable, currently outstanding economic position. TRR should become the programme's shared proof-of-rights architecture, while TSR specializes it for securities and SPE closes settled claims.

title: Token-Standard Selection for Financial Claims and Receipts
subtitle: ERC-1155, ERC-6909, ERC-3525 and controlled securities interfaces in an institutional registry
abstract: Choosing a token standard is an engineering and lifecycle decision—not a legal classification of the underlying instrument. The same claim may be technically representable as a fungible class, a token-by-ID balance, a semi-fungible slot, or a controlled securities token. The correct selection depends on holder granularity, legal assignment rules, encumbrances, lifecycle partitioning, transfer restrictions, and the economics of reconciliation.

evidence.heading: Standards have different unit models
evidence.body: ERC-6909 defines a minimal multi-token interface with per-ID balances and operators. ERC-3525 introduces a slot-and-value model associated with token IDs, enabling partial values within related categories. ERC-1155 provides a mature multi-token ecosystem for fungible and non-fungible IDs. ERC-7518 and other regulated-asset proposals introduce additional compliant and authorization interfaces, but implementation status, dependencies and contract-level guarantees must be assessed separately. None of these standards alone performs KYC, insolvency segregation or beneficial-owner recordkeeping.

evidence.heading: Legal design is upstream of interface design
evidence.body: The SEC staff's 2026 treatment of tokenized securities underscores why investor rights and issuer arrangements must precede interface choice. Project Guardian's institutional frameworks likewise focus on the fund lifecycle, on-chain registers, custody and asset servicing rather than treating issuance as the whole product. Choosing token ID structures before defining the authoritative unit of ownership risks making a technical representation expensive or impossible to reconcile with the actual registrar.

evidence.heading: Ecosystem support versus financial invariants
evidence.body: The most gas-efficient standard is not necessarily the least costly institutional model. A minimal interface can decrease transfer overhead but require more custom access controls, indexers and corporate-action tooling. A semi-fungible standard can encode tranche or maturity attributes but complicate exchange and custodian integration. The proper decision compares total implementation and operating costs, threat surface, event semantics, auditability and lifecycle extensibility—not contract deployment cost alone.

architecture.heading: Representing the unit of entitlement
architecture.body: Before selecting ERC interfaces, define whether a single unit means one legal share, one USD of principal, one percentage of a fund, or one contractual claim whose value may change. Then define how rights split and merge, how beneficial holders are enumerated, and whether the rights registry accepts transfer decisions by wallet alone. For controlled securities a token may represent a distinct transferable position and still require registrar validation and issuer-controlled restrictions.

architecture.heading: ERC-1155 / ERC-6909: class balance patterns
architecture.body: A class token model maintains balances keyed by token type or series. ERC-1155's multi-token conventions can be advantageous for wallets and marketplace integrations; ERC-6909 offers a minimal interface for multiple types. Financial risks arise when a single ID aggregates legally different claims—such as series with different liens or redemption dates—or when arbitrary fractional units hide a varying conversion ratio. Use immutable class metadata and a versioned entitlement registry.

architecture.heading: ERC-3525: slot and value are not a substitute for servicing
architecture.body: The slot/value model suits partially transferable positions grouped by shared characteristics, such as maturity or coupon schedule. However, value transfers do not automatically update the bond register, payment agent, collateral encumbrance ledger or eligibility restrictions. Assign a legally meaningful instrument ID and avoid treating a slot as proof of all associated legal terms. If a position is split, the register must reconcile old and new holder identities and values.

architecture.heading: Compliance extensions and failure permissions
architecture.body: Assess restricted transfer, freeze, forced transfer, upgrade, pause and recovery interfaces. Their existence is not evidence of appropriateness: emergency authority can be a necessary compliance feature and also a governance concentration risk. Decide who can operate each control, under what signed policy, with what notice and audit trail. ERC-7943 and ERC-7518 are useful research references for possible interface designs, but not regulatory approval or production assurance.

case.title: Worked selection matrix: three synthetic instruments
case.setup: Three instruments share a common platform but not a common legal unit: Series A USD 250,000 bond principal split into many positions, Fund B 2,000 shares with daily NAV, and Receipt C backed by 500 deposited equities.
rows: Units of principal with maturity and coupons
Rights registry for principal, coupon and encumbrance
Unified evidence schema; separate issuer obligations
case.formula: Normalized represented quantity = token balance × declared unit conversion; backing ratio = eligible independent backing units ÷ outstanding receipt entitlement units.
case.interpretation: The model supports interoperable recordkeeping without implying that heterogeneous legal rights become fungible just because one token standard can represent them.

risks: Identifier aliasing
Two legally distinct tranches share a token ID and secondary transfers cross an instrument boundary.
Immutable legal instrument identifiers and explicit series partitioning.
Privilege concentration
Upgradeable compliance roles can mint, seize, freeze or alter balances without institutional approval.
Multisignature or threshold governance, separation of duties and emergency audit.
Investor-facing compatibility
Wallets display balances but not eligibility, NAV, coupon ownership or beneficial interests.
A rights-aware application layer and machine-readable instrument disclosure.
tests: Implement the same synthetic claim with ERC-1155, ERC-6909 and ERC-3525 representations; compare event volume, complexity and gas, not solely initial deployment.
Introduce a restricted holder transfer, split/merge and partial redemption; verify registrar and token balances after each event.
Test role revocation, contract upgrade, pause, recovery and external supply attestation using a threat-model worksheet.
conclusion: TRR should define the rights and reconciliation model independently of any ERC token interface. Token standards then become replaceable representations selected by lifecycle requirements, liquidity integration and controls. A controlled security token is a governed financial system, not just a specialized balance map.

title: Issue, Mint, Transfer, Redeem and Burn: A Verifiable Token Lifecycle
subtitle: State machines, event correlation, disputed positions and independently reconstructed supply
abstract: A token lifecycle spans more than the familiar mint and burn entry points. It begins when a legally valid economic position is originated and authenticated, and it ends only when the position has been extinguished or validly transferred out of the modeled system. This report defines a state-machine approach with explicit preconditions, durable evidence, and invariants for cross-system completeness.

evidence.heading: Lifecycle coverage is a documented infrastructure problem
evidence.body: The BIS Project Promissa demonstrates why financial commitments need issuance, modification, encashment and archival states rather than a single transferable token. Project Guardian's institutional material addresses the full lifecycle of funds, including on-chain registers and asset servicing. IMF analysis on market inefficiencies similarly assesses tokenization across issuance, trading and post-trade functions. These sources support the lifecycle approach, but TSP-01's exact state machine is a design proposal, not a property proven by the cited prototypes.

evidence.heading: Token confirmations do not prove economic completeness
evidence.body: Smart-contract event receipts show that specified code executed under the chain's assumptions. They do not show that all relevant off-chain obligations were included, that no custodian asset was withdrawn, or that every legal transfer was authorized. The FSB identifies operational, liquidity and interconnectedness vulnerabilities. For a rights-bearing token, verification must also include source completeness, permissible state transitions and the ledger of extinguished positions.

evidence.heading: Operations need compensation as well as reversal
evidence.body: In a hybrid payment system, the money leg and the token leg may have different finality rules and recovery options. A token burn may be irreversible while a payment instruction is still rejectable, or vice versa. A recovery protocol must therefore distinguish an aborted workflow, a compensated financial event and a legal claim for restitution. Simply retrying a timed-out transaction can create duplicate payment or double release.

architecture.heading: Formal states and guards
architecture.body: Model an instrument through Draft, Verified, Issued, Outstanding, Restricted, PendingRedemption, Redeemed and Cancelled states, with Disputed and Suspended as cross-cutting conditions. A successful mint requires a verified asset or claim and authorization to create supply. Transfer requires eligible recipient, valid mandate and transferable ownership. Redeem requires an accepted cancellation instruction and an agreed rule for when the economic claim is discharged. Burn is not automatically equivalent to lawful redemption.

architecture.heading: Three independent ledgers
architecture.body: Maintain an economic-rights ledger (instrument and legal holders), a token-state ledger (balances, contracts and on-chain events) and a settlement/accounting ledger (money movement, liabilities and journals). Reconcile them with a shared economic-event ID. The issuer cannot certify population completeness by checking token supply alone; auditors need independently sourced claims, asset backing or custodian statements against which token balances are measured.

architecture.heading: Partial settlement and partitions
architecture.body: Partition available rights into freely transferable, encumbered, disputed, restricted, pending-redemption and redeemed quantities. Rights should never be double-counted across partitions. For payment claims, only approved balances may become freely transferable tokenized claims. For custody-backed receipts, blocked holdings must remain represented in custody and legal rights even if tokens are transferred into an escrow or freeze state.

architecture.heading: Recovery without fabricating finality
architecture.body: Use idempotent instructions and a unique settlement ID, persistent state transitions, measured confirmation timeouts and explicit incomplete states. When a bank rail confirms payment but the token ledger fails, it may be inappropriate to reverse the bank entry; recovery can require issuing a legally authorized replacement token or initiating compensation. Each exception must preserve the audit trail rather than rewriting history.

case.title: Worked ledger: a partially redeemed tokenized bond
case.setup: A synthetic debt instrument has USD 1,000,000 issued principal represented by 10,000 units of USD 100 each. USD 200,000 is pledged as collateral; a USD 150,000 redemption is proposed from unencumbered holdings.
rows: 8,500 token units outstanding; 2,000 pledged remain within outstanding supply
case.formula: Principal outstanding = issued principal − legally completed redemptions = 1,000,000 − 150,000 = 850,000. Outstanding units = 8,500, including 2,000 restricted units.
case.interpretation: Restrictions change the availability of units but do not necessarily change economic outstanding principal. Burning a restricted unit without the secured party's authority could destroy token state while leaving a legally enforceable security interest.

risks: Replay and double issuance
A failed acknowledgement causes the issuer to retry mint with a new ID and double available supply.
Deterministic issuance IDs, idempotency keys and independent issuer/rights reconciliation.
Incorrect release of collateral
Pledged units move despite a collateral agreement restricting transfer.
Partition-level authorization and enforceable release evidence from secured party.
Cash-token timing split
Payer releases cash, then cancellation is delayed or fails.
Pending-redemption lock, finality proof and exception/compensation process.
tests: Construct a property-based state-machine test that attempts all transitions from every state, expecting invalid transitions to be rejected.
Fault-inject payment failures and duplicate chain logs; require eventual accounting consistency without creating counterfeit claims.
Have an independent simulated auditor rebuild outstanding positions solely from authoritative claims, verified events and signed settlement results.
conclusion: The invariant that matters is not that tokens can be burned: every action must preserve the relationship among legal rights, custody or liability backing, transferability and final monetary discharge. The canonical lifecycle should be a reusable foundation for TRR, TSR and SPE across the programme.
